Thereunto
thair-un-TOO
adv.
From there and unto: to that; to it. Webster 1828: to that; to this. Peter uses it twice for the Christian’s calling, and both times what he is called to is something no one would volunteer for.

Biblical Definition

Peter uses this word to attach a calling to a duty that runs against nature. Having forbidden retaliation he adds the ground: Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing (1 Peter 3:9). The Christian does not merely refrain from returning insult; he blesses, and he does so because that is the thing he was called to. Paul uses it of affliction with the same finality: That no man should be moved by these afflictions: for yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto (1 Thessalonians 3:3). Afflictions are not an interruption to the appointment; they are the appointment. The word also fixes the manner of prayer to its object: Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints (Ephesians 6:18) — the last clause of the armour passage, and the one that makes the rest usable. Peter puts the same construction at the head of his great passage on Christ’s example: For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example (1 Peter 2:21).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines THEREUNTO as to that; to this — a compound adverb joining a verb to its object at a distance, and characteristic of the Authorized Version’s connective style.

expand to see more

THEREUNTO, adv. — To that; to this.

Compare THEREUPON, upon that; THEREOF, of that; THEREIN, in that.

THEREUNTO is now archaic in speech but survives in legal English.

It renders a Greek relative-with-preposition compactly, keeping the antecedent clear.

From there and unto.

Key Scripture

1 Peter 3:9 — "Not rendering evil for evil, or railing for railing: but contrariwise blessing; knowing that ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing."

1 Thessalonians 3:3 — "That no man should be moved by these afflictions: for yourselves know that we are appointed thereunto."

Ephesians 6:18 — "Praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit, and watching thereunto with all perseverance and supplication for all saints;"

1 Peter 2:21 — "For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps:"

Modern Corruption

1 Thessalonians 3:3 says believers are appointed to affliction, which is the plain denial of the teaching that suffering in a Christian’s life indicates a failure of faith.

expand to see more

We are appointed thereunto. Paul sends Timothy to Thessalonica specifically so that no one would be moved by the afflictions, and his stabilizing argument is not that the trouble will pass but that it was assigned. This is the flat contradiction of prosperity teaching, which must treat sustained affliction as evidence of insufficient faith, a hidden sin, or a failure to claim what is available. It also corrects a gentler error common among the orthodox — the assumption that a well-ordered Christian life should be largely free of trouble, so that trouble prompts the question what have I done wrong? Scripture’s answer is often nothing; Job’s comforters were rebuked for assuming otherwise. The 1689 Confession speaks of God leaving His children for a season to manifold temptations for holy ends, and Acts 14:22 tells the disciples plainly that through much tribulation we must enter into the kingdom.

1 Peter 3:9 is the harder command in practice. It is not enough to withhold the retort; the believer is to bless, and the reason given is that he was called to this. The therapeutic vocabulary now available for these situations — boundaries, toxicity, the duty to protect oneself — is not simply wrong about everything (Scripture knows about avoiding a foolish man and about lawful self-protection), but it supplies no category whatever for blessing the reviler, which is the actual apostolic command. Where that vocabulary becomes the church’s working ethic, 1 Peter 3:9 becomes unpreachable. And the ground Peter gives is not that blessing works, but that the blesser will inherit a blessing.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eis touto, unto this; kaleo (G2564), to call; keimai (G2749), to be set or appointed; agrupneo (G69), to keep awake, to watch.

expand to see more

Greek eis touto — unto this, to that end; the phrase rendered thereunto and hereunto in Peter.

Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call; the calling to which the believer is thereunto called (1 Peter 3:9).

Greek keimai (G2749) — to lie, to be laid down or appointed; we are appointed thereunto (1 Thessalonians 3:3).

Greek agrupneo (G69) — to be sleepless, to keep watch; watching thereunto (Ephesians 6:18).

Greek hupogrammos (G5261) — a writing-copy set for a child to trace; the example Christ leaves (1 Peter 2:21).

Usage

"Ye are thereunto called, that ye should inherit a blessing (1 Peter 3:9) — not merely withholding the retort, but blessing."

"We are appointed thereunto (1 Thessalonians 3:3) — affliction is the appointment, not an interruption to it."

"Watching thereunto with all perseverance (Ephesians 6:18) — the clause that makes the rest of the armour usable."
